WarningKnown limitations: Dataverse infrastructure





These impact metrics undercount real scholarly reach due to known infrastructure issues being addressed in an ongoing Dataverse migration:

Dataverse 5.14 DataCite export bug: The publication metadata field (paper DOI linked by depositors) is not exported to DataCite as relatedIdentifiers. As a result, UCLA Dataverse datasets show 0 citations in DataCite, even when they are cited. Citation counts here are retrieved directly from OpenAlex as a workaround.
Make Data Count (MDC) not enabled: Per-dataset view and download metrics are unavailable. Only aggregate download totals are reported.
Restricted and draft datasets excluded: ~562 of 942 datasets in the index are inaccessible without authentication and are not included in this analysis.
ISBN-linked datasets not tracked: 160 datasets are linked to book chapters (via ISBN). These represent real scholarship connections, mostly from large archaeology collections, but citation counts are not retrievable via OpenAlex.
Depositor coverage gap: ~200 publicly accessible datasets have no publication link at all. Improving intake guidance for depositors would increase coverage.

Expected improvements after migration to Dataverse 6.x: DataCite relatedIdentifiers export fixed, MDC enablement possible.



See also: Consulting → one-on-one consultations · Instruction → workshop attendance · About & methodology







NoteData notes






AWS usage: Cost Explorer API (last 12 months) merged with historical CSV exports, shown as each application’s relative share of monthly spend rather than dollar amounts. Most recent 1–2 months are estimates; final billing may differ
Dataverse datasets/files/downloads: Cumulative counts from the UCLA Dataverse /api/info/metrics endpoint — stored in data/raw/infrastructure/datasets_files_published_monthly.csv
Downloads: File-level events as reported by Dataverse. Includes automated and bot traffic; not filtered for human-only access
S3 storage: Fetched live from AWS CloudWatch at render time. May be unavailable without valid AWS credentials; CloudWatch reports storage metrics once daily
Traceable publication links: Publication DOIs from Dataverse metadata API; citation counts from OpenAlex. Undercounts real impact; see the limitations note above.

title: Consulting and project support
text:
Student project work
DataSquad students documented 204 project tasks from 2023 to 2025. A task is one piece of follow-on project work tracked on the team’s Trello board, such as cleaning a dataset, writing code, or preparing a map, after a consultation turned into a project. Tasks are not consultations and are not added to the consultation counts. Tracking on Trello became routine in 2023, so earlier project work is not counted.

Deaths in custody: DataSquad students merged and reconciled several sources into a national dataset the lab now maintains and updates itself.

title: Research Supported by Shared Investments
text:
DSC buys data, runs platforms, and maintains computing that individual labs could not easily provide for themselves. These shared investments support identifiable research, and each needs ongoing data, access, and technical stewardship to keep working. Two of UCLA’s six 2024 Public Impact Research Award recipients led research that DSC supported (UCLA Newsroom).
Researchers own the scholarship; DSC supplied the documented data, access, or computing described below.

title: Research Supported by Shared Investments
text:
Voter file and governed access (Redivis)







Research barrier
National voter history arrives as thousands of state files, over 10 TB, too large to store and process locally and too inconsistent to analyze as delivered. The records contain personal information such as names and addresses, so the data has to be held securely, and its license requires governed access.


DSC investment
Acquired the L2 national voter file with a Library subject selector. DSC’s Jamie Jamison scripted the data ingest for a doctoral curator, who made it analysis-ready as one national table, and set up the data use agreement and user management. DSC provides governed access through Redivis, a platform for restricted research data.


Documented use
Redivis at UCLA: ~20TB of protected data, 50 registered users, and 150+ workflows (users and workflows, not projects). Research uses named publicly: election administration, gentrification, Latino voting, and a project linking voter records with health records.


Research outputs
See the verified outputs below: the FORCE11 2024 presentation and an award-winning dissertation on U.S. election administration.


Evidence of the connection
A 2024 conference presentation co-given by the platform’s founder and the UCLA curator; a paper using the L2 voter file that thanks the curator for access.


Coverage and limits
Drawn from the presentation and the public work of the researchers it names. Not yet a census of Redivis projects.


Continuing requirement
Data license renewal, platform subscription, curation of new releases, access administration, and onboarding for new researchers.

title: Research Supported by Shared Investments
text:
Research computing







Research barrier
Some datasets exceed what a lab can host or process on its own machines.


DSC investment
Hosts research servers and a deep learning machine, with staff and student support for processing and training.


Documented use
Multi-year support for the Carceral Ecologies lab’s helicopter-surveillance analysis.


Research outputs
One measured data-loading step fell from about 318 minutes to about 2 (claim #1), a service improvement that supported the research rather than an output of it. The lab’s research was later recognized by a 2024 UCLA Public Impact Research Award.


Evidence of the connection
Case record and the researcher’s own account, shared with permission.


Coverage and limits
One engagement shown; a second (machine-learning analysis of animal behavior) awaits the researcher’s confirmation. Job logs have not been compiled.


Continuing requirement
Hardware maintenance, system administration, and staff who can support researchers on it.

title: Research Supported by Shared Investments
text:
UCLA Dataverse



Research barrier
Researchers need a trusted place to deposit, cite, and share data, and UCLA’s legacy social science archive needed a modern home.


DSC investment
Operates UCLA Dataverse with campus sign-in, DOI minting, and preservation, and harvested the legacy social science archive into it.


Documented use
~1,390 released datasets (February 2026), including about 1,014 legacy archive datasets, with download activity on the infrastructure evidence page.


Research outputs
Publications that depositors linked to their datasets are listed as traceable publication links.


Evidence of the connection
DOI relationships supplied by depositors.


Coverage and limits
Depositors do not always link publications, and a linked paper is often the depositor’s own, so these links are not a measure of reuse.


Continuing requirement
Platform operation, storage, curation, and DOI services.

title: Research Supported by Shared Investments
text:
LARIAC aerial imagery and LiDAR



Research barrier
High-resolution aerial imagery and LiDAR for Los Angeles County is costly and licensed through a consortium of public agencies.


DSC investment
UCLA is a member of the Los Angeles Region Imagery Acquisition Consortium (LARIAC) through the Library, and DSC is how the UCLA community gets the data: imagery, LiDAR, elevation models, and building footprints, free to UCLA researchers on request (DSC access guide). DSC also provisions EagleView imagery accounts.


Documented use
8 to 12 active EagleView users a year (2023 to 2026). Researchers from environment and sustainability, geography, and engineering, and campus Facilities for planning.


Research outputs
A 2025 npj Natural Hazards study by UCLA authors built on 2020 LARIAC LiDAR (see below).


Evidence of the connection
The paper states its LiDAR source; UCLA’s access to LARIAC runs through DSC.


Coverage and limits
Papers rarely name how they obtained the data. Other UCLA papers use LARIAC-derived products that may circulate outside the license, so they are not counted.


Continuing requirement
Consortium membership, data storage, access administration, and account provisioning.

title: Research Supported by Shared Investments
text:
GIS and geospatial support
DSC’s GIS librarian left in August 2024 and the position was never refilled. GIS requests continued.
Geography was DSC’s single largest departmental workshop audience from 2020 to April 2024: 64 of the 1,575 UCLA-affiliated workshop attendance records from 2020 to April 2024, more than any other department over that period as a whole.
Until they left for a faculty position in August 2024, DSC’s GIS librarian handled 72 to 82 booked consultations a year (2021 to 2023) across Urban Planning, Public Affairs, Environment and Sustainability, and Digital Humanities. They also co-taught a graduate Public Health course, ran systemwide UC GIS workshops that reached 617 participants in 2023 alone, and managed key research datasets, including the LARIAC aerial imagery. That demand hasn’t gone away. DSC still fields GIS requests, just without the specialist capacity to meet them.
For context, 81 of 187 Carnegie R1 institutions (43%) maintain a dedicated GIS librarian, rising to 81% among the top 25 R&D-spending universities.
The campus mapping platform is a separate gap, a matter of ownership rather than consultation demand. UCLA’s ArcGIS Online platform, used across Geography, Luskin, Fielding, Digital Humanities, Political Science, and Social Data Science, has over 7,100 accounts and more than 3,000 active users in the past year, per an OARC governance report from December 2025. As of that report, with no designated administrator, it was running at over 200% of its licensed storage.

title: Research Supported by Shared Investments
text:
3D capture and Potree
Doug Daniels, DSC’s emerging technologies librarian, was named UCLA’s 2026 LAUC-LA Librarian of the Year.
The award, one of two given university-wide by LAUC-LA in a 15-nomination, peer-selected cycle, recognized partnerships across archaeology, digital humanities, medical sciences, materials science, and Egyptology, including the Refugee Material Culture Initiative (Research enabled) and a drone survey of Iceland’s Mosfell Valley with a doctoral student from the Cotsen Institute of Archaeology. A separate Lux Lab collaboration, a surgical probe holder built with an undergraduate student, is now in clinical use at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center.
pointcloud.ucla.edu, the Potree-based viewer DSC runs alongside Dataverse, is what turns this work into something researchers can use rather than just store: 3D scans and point-cloud data become interactive models, explorable in a browser instead of sitting as a static file in an archive.

“Daniels’ work has strengthened partnerships across campus and throughout the greater Los Angeles community while helping students succeed with their individual research projects.” — Patrick Lavey, LAUC-LA Award Committee Chair, UCLA Newsroom

title: Research Supported by Shared Investments
text:
How outputs were selected
We reviewed each investment’s available records: project records, the public work of researchers named in DSC presentations, depositor links in UCLA Dataverse, and a full-text search of OpenAlex for LARIAC. An output is listed only when a public output exists and its connection to the investment is supported by an explicit citation, acknowledgment, or methods statement, or by a project record confirmed by the researcher, and when the researcher has agreed to be named. Citation counts and researcher prominence did not affect selection. Outputs still being confirmed, including work on machine-learning analysis of animal behavior and three further LARIAC papers, are not shown.

title: Research Capability Built
text:
What the teaching record shows
DSC instruction grew from workshops for its own campus into instruction co-run across the University of California, and it trained campus volunteers who went on to lead much of the teaching. The evidence covers workshops from May 2017 through September 2026 and counts registrations and sessions, not individual learning outcomes.

title: Research Capability Built
section: A program example: the UC Carpentries network
text:
A program example: the UC Carpentries network
What it is. In 2020 DSC co-founded the systemwide UC Carpentries network with partner campuses at Berkeley, San Diego, Santa Barbara, Merced, and Riverside, turning a single-campus workshop program into instruction delivered across the University of California.
What DSC does. Co-coordinates the series, recruits and trains instructors, and co-delivers workshops. Campus volunteers trained through the program now lead much of the teaching.
Scale. The UC Carpentries series drew 10,749 registered seats from 2020 through September 2026 (see the seat table on the instruction evidence page).
Limits. Registrations are not people or attendance, the audience spans all participating campuses, and credit for the network is shared with its partners. Individual learning outcomes are not measured here.






ImportantWhat this pattern means, and what it cannot mean




It means DSC instruction reached a large and changing audience: its own campus through 2019, then UC-wide online series from 2020, with campus-trained volunteers teaching alongside staff.
It cannot mean that 27,986 people were trained. A registered seat is one registration for one session. One person who registers for four sessions counts four times, and many registrants do not attend.
Attendance is recorded only for some series. Where it exists, compare attended with registered seats within that series and those dates only. The UC Carpentries ratio (about 1 attended per 3 registered) does not transfer to other series or to the total.
UCLA participants are a subset. The UC-wide series include other campuses’ registrants; UCLA-only figures are on the instruction evidence page.
The lower 2025-2026 bars are not a measure of demand. 2026 is partial, and neither GIS Week nor Love Data Week has counted DSC seats in those years (DSC was not involved in GIS Week in 2024-2025, while its GIS position was unfilled).









NoteThe long view (history, as of 2026)



Instruction went through three eras. From 2017 the unit taught locally, one campus, in person, and by January 2020 campus volunteers trained through the program were leading the workshops. In 2020 online delivery made it possible to teach across campuses without travel, and the systemwide UC Carpentries network was co-founded in response, with Berkeley, San Diego, Santa Barbara, Merced, and Riverside as partners. From 2023 that network operated at system scale. Read the teaching section of the history

title: Research Capability Built
text:
Open-science lessons and research software
Two outside awards support this work: an IMLS grant to UCLA and a Sloan Foundation grant to the multi-campus UC OSPO Network.
DSC’s open source program office (OSPO) work, licensing review, repository best practices, and release guidance, is part of the UC OSPO Network, funded by a $1.85M Sloan Foundation grant to the network as a whole (a multi-campus award, not a grant to DSC). It exists because the need is real: a 2025 scan of roughly 81,000 UC-affiliated code repositories found 77.5% carried no license at all, meaning most UC research code cannot legally be reused or built on.
Alongside it, a $237,839 IMLS grant (Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian Program, RE-252335-OLS-22) funded an open science curriculum built by and for librarians: 15 peer-reviewed lessons (14 were proposed), each with a DOI, developed by two cohorts across 2023-2024. Tim Dennis served as Program Director, Todd Grappone as Co-PI, and Zhiyuan Yao, DSC’s GIS librarian at the time, as Program Coordinator. All lessons are built on The Carpentries Workbench and released under CC-BY 4.0; one, DMP 101, has already been formally adopted into the Library Carpentry curriculum, with the rest in active community piloting.
That curriculum work sits inside a larger, ongoing commitment: Dennis co-chairs the Library Carpentry Governance Group, which sets lesson-adoption and curriculum-quality standards for the global Library Carpentry program, not just UCLA’s. DSC staff maintain or co-maintain lessons taught worldwide, from core Carpentries material (Unix Shell, Tidy Data, R, Python, Computational Thinking) to newer additions in qualitative data methods, data management, Wikidata, data archiving, and AI, including a published lesson on using AI coding agents in research while preserving validation and reproducibility (agentic-research-workflows). Dennis is also a Center for Open Science Ambassador (2016-present) and was teaching faculty for the Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in the Social Sciences’ Research Transparency and Reproducibility Training.

title: Research Capability Built
text:
DataSquad: student consultants
DataSquad logged 111 reportable project tasks in 2025.
DataSquad is DSC’s peer-consulting model: undergraduate and graduate student consultants providing sustained project support alongside DSC staff’s direct consultations. Much of its work is sustained, hands-on project support rather than one-off questions. Task tracking in Trello began in 2023, so the rise from 6 tasks that year partly reflects record-keeping, not only more work.
The program started in 2020 on a gift from Norman Powell, which funded student salaries and laptops for the first cohort, and became a formal program in 2021. The Library added funding in 2023 to expand the team and add in-person hours. In 2024, DataSquad absorbed the LuxLab student program after its funding source, CLICC funds, became restricted, merging two student-support lines into one.
It also prepares students for data careers. DSC documented post-graduation destinations for ten DataSquad graduates from 2023–2025, and all of them found placements, at employers including McKinsey & Company, Amazon, World Wide Technology, and CVS Health. That is a tracked group, not an outcome rate for every student in the program. Several of the same students worked on DataSquad’s highest-profile faculty projects before landing those placements. Lawrence Lee, who built the codebooks the BioCritical Studies Lab uses to update its dataset, is now a Software Development Engineer at Amazon.

title: Research Capability Built
section: 2017 to 2026: what was built, and when capacity changed

title: Research Enabled by DSC
text: UCLA researchers have used DSC for data and technical work that crosses lab and department boundaries. At least 1,908 confirmed UCLA researchers used its instruction or consultation from 2017 to September 2026. DSC also made a 10 TB national voter file analysis-ready, provides governed access to restricted data, and operates UCLA’s research-data repository. Its staff time, counting DSC staff and time contributed by other Library units, fell from 5.7 FTE in 2022-23 to 4.0 in 2025-26. The question for the university is who will be accountable for these functions as DSC’s capacity changes: connecting them, setting standards, maintaining the infrastructure, and carrying the expertise forward.

title: Research Enabled by DSC
text:
What the evidence establishes
DSC’s work shows up in research outputs, not only in service counts. Three documented collaborations on the Research enabled page show different kinds of DSC support: data preparation and computing for a helicopter-surveillance study, where one data-loading step went from about 318 minutes to about 2; a national deaths-in-custody dataset a lab now updates itself; and 3D capture of a refugee boat for a humanities initiative. More are on the shared investments page. How cases are selected.

Shared investments pathway




Since 1961. UCLA has kept research data for reuse since 1961, when political scientist Dwaine Marvick founded the Political Behavior Archive. The unit’s name and institutional home have changed several times since; what persisted is the stewardship of research data and the work of widening access to it. Read the history
The materials have changed, from survey datasets to large and restricted files, spatial imagery, 3D models, and research code, and the archive’s knowledge now shapes how DSC helps researchers work with them during a project and how the results stay understandable and usable afterward. DSC does not archive everything it supports. Its role is to connect consultation, computing, access, and the repository so that valuable outputs have a path to reuse. How the functions connect

title: Research Enabled
text:
Three collaborations
These three were chosen to show different kinds of documented support, not typical outcomes: data preparation and computing, a dataset a lab maintains itself, and 3D capture. For scale and breadth, see the consultation series above, the instruction pathway, and the shared investments page.

Police helicopter surveillance (Carceral Ecologies)

Research need The lab’s flight-tracking data outgrew what it could host and process itself. What DSC did Cleaned and integrated the flight data, advised on spatial analysis, refactored the R code, and moved the work onto DSC computing. What the research gained Analyzable flight tables joined to Los Angeles neighborhoods, and one data-loading step cut from about 318 minutes to about 2. What still depends on DSC The hosted R server and technical help as the lab’s data keeps growing.

The Carceral Ecologies lab, directed by Nicholas Shapiro in UCLA’s Institute for Society and Genetics, studies the health and mental-health effects of law-enforcement helicopter surveillance across Los Angeles County from 2017 through 2022 (lab project page). Its public findings include that LAPD helicopters fly lowest over largely Black and Hispanic neighborhoods, with a median of about 550 feet over Watts at night (CalMatters, July 2024).
When COVID closed the prisons where the lab had done environmental field sampling, Shapiro moved its work to data analysis, and the flight-trajectory dataset soon outgrew what the lab could host itself. In his words, DSC and DataSquad supported the lab “through technical assistance, helping one of my research students (who became staff) grow her R skills, and in hosting the R server that makes this research possible.”
A student researcher on the team first learned R and GIS from DSC staff in a 2019 African American Studies course taught with DSC. In 2022 she came back with the team’s flight-tracking data, twelve monthly files of about a million rows each, and met DSC staff and DataSquad consultants more than 30 times that year (her 2023 interview). Together they converted the raw flight records into analyzable tables, identified individual flights, filtered out impossible altitude readings, and joined millions of positions to Los Angeles neighborhoods (her analysis code). DSC’s GIS librarian advised on the spatial analysis, recommending a density-based clustering method for classifying the flight data and helping fix geometry problems in the spatial files. When the processing outgrew her laptop that fall, DSC moved the data onto its deep learning machine and gave her access to its hosted R server.
As the lab acquired more data, DSC helped it scale. In March 2023 DSC staff met with Shapiro’s team, set up the lab’s new statistician on the deep learning machine, and loaded five years of additional data the lab had purchased. Over the following months DSC staff and DataSquad students worked with the statistician to process the dataset in batches and speed up elevation lookups about tenfold by switching data sources (shared code). One measured piece of that work cut the time to load the data from about 318 minutes to about 2 (DataSquad project page). DSC staff on the collaboration included Tim Dennis, Leigh Phan, Zhiyuan Yao, and Kristian Allen.
In Shapiro’s account, the lab’s ability to keep analyzing its growing flight data has depended on that technical help and on the R server DSC hosts.

“This work wouldn’t have happened without your team!”
Nicholas Shapiro, director of Carceral Ecologies, November 2024 (quoted with permission)

The research and its findings belong to the lab; Shapiro received a 2024 UCLA Public Impact Research Award for it (Institute for Society and Genetics, August 2024).


Deaths in custody (BioCritical Studies Lab)

Research need No single, reliable national dataset of deaths in custody existed. What DSC did DataSquad students merged and reconciled the sources, found missed deaths, built maps and dashboards, and wrote codebooks for new data. What the research gained A national dataset the lab maintains, with tools it uses to update the data itself. What still depends on DSC Recurring DataSquad work as the sources change and are revised.

In January 2021, Terence Keel’s BioCritical Studies Lab, in UCLA’s Institute for Society and Genetics, set out to build a single dataset of deaths in custody across the United States from 2000 to 2020. Those deaths are reported by several crowd-based sources, including The Guardian, Fatal Encounters, and Mapping Police Violence, each with its own variables and standards, and the dataset has to be revised as the sources change.
DataSquad students Julia Wood and Ethan Allavarpu merged the sources, reconciled discrepancies between them, and identified deaths that some sources had missed. They then built maps and dashboards, including Los Angeles maps, and ran statistical comparisons of death rates that, in the words of the lab’s assistant director, were “instrumental in informing us which locations we should prioritize” (UCLA Library, May 2022). DSC staff later helped the lab organize and document its data. In 2024 DataSquad student Lawrence Lee developed two codebooks that let the lab integrate and clean new data from any source, and taught the lab to use them so it could update the dataset on its own.
Keeping the national dataset usable through new sources and revisions has depended on recurring DataSquad work and on tools the lab learned to use itself.

“There is a lack of comprehensive and reliable data on death in custody in the United States, and the work the DataSquad has done has helped us address this need and has allowed us to maintain this dataset over time and through revisions.”
Grace Sosa, assistant director, BioCritical Studies Lab, August 2024 (quoted with permission)

In the same letter, Sosa writes that the lab has used the dataset to complete projects funded by the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The research is the lab’s; Keel, like Shapiro, received a 2024 UCLA Public Impact Research Award (Institute for Society and Genetics, August 2024).


3D capture for the humanities (Refugee Material Culture Initiative)

Research need Preserve refugee art and artifacts digitally, for a museum exhibit and for teaching. What DSC did 3D scanned the Boat of Hope, processed the models, and set up a web viewer. What the research gained A public 3D model anyone can explore in a browser. What still depends on DSC Continued hosting on pointcloud.ucla.edu, a server DSC built and runs.

Classics professor Kelly Nguyen’s Refugee Material Culture Initiative, a collaboration with the Vietnamese Heritage Museum in Garden Grove, digitally preserves art and artifacts made and used by refugees (Cotsen Institute of Archaeology). Doug Daniels, DSC’s emerging technologies librarian, 3D scanned the “Boat of Hope,” a six-meter river sampan that carried nine refugees out of Vietnam in 1984, and prepared the models for the museum’s digital exhibit (the initiative’s page on Doug).
Explore the Boat of Hope and its story in 3D
In Nguyen’s course “Decolonizing Refugee Data from Rome to Vietnam,” students build digital exhibitions from artifacts like these. Nguyen, working with Doug, also organized a digital archaeology day that brought more than 50 Westminster High School students and more than 30 elders from Little Saigon to campus (UCLA Humanities, April 2026; UCLA Newsroom, July 2026).
Doug also spent two weeks in Iceland’s Mosfell Valley running drone surveys for a doctoral student at the Cotsen Institute of Archaeology (UCLA Newsroom, July 2026). He processed data as it arrived during fieldwork and set up a library workstation so the student could keep working after returning; student employee Connor Lim processed the survey data once it came back.
The boat model lives on pointcloud.ucla.edu, a server Doug built in 2022 so that anyone can explore 3D data in an ordinary web browser, as does Iceland turf-architecture survey data; student employee Bianca Badajos helped set up its Potree viewer. Publishing processed data there lets researchers examine it without specialized hardware and lets instructors bring it into class.
The public boat model depends on DSC’s capture, processing, and continued hosting, alongside the initiative’s and the museum’s stewardship of the boat and its story.
The scholarship belongs to Nguyen’s initiative and the Cotsen researchers. Doug was named a 2026 UCLA Librarian of the Year for his work across campus (UCLA Newsroom, July 2026).






NoteThe long view (history, as of 2026)



The archive answered research questions from its early years: data discovery, codebooks, and help with statistical software. The 2018 redesign widened consulting to the whole research life cycle, from data management plans to publication and preservation, and added GIS, 3D capture, machine learning, research software, and reproducible workflows. From about 2023 the work shifted from single appointments toward project support that ran for months. Read the consulting section of the history

title: About This Site
text:
This site shows what research capacity the UCLA Library Data Science Center (DSC) has built, and the evidence behind each figure. It is written for campus leadership, faculty, and library and research administrators weighing how DSC’s functions will be carried forward, not as an internal service dashboard.
This site documents the work and the records behind it. The home page and the three pathway pages (Research enabled, Research capability built, and Shared investments) make the argument; the evidence pages (Consulting, Instruction, Infrastructure) hold the underlying records. Every headline figure has an entry in the project’s claim register, which records its approved wording, time window, unit, and source, and a check in the build refuses to publish a headline figure without one.
The research examples are illustrative, not representative, and the research in them belongs to the labs and initiatives named. People are named only with permission or where they are DSC staff or student employees credited for their own work.
It is rendered from source data and published as a static site on GitHub Pages.

title: About This Site
text:
Definitions
Consultation A direct interaction between a DSC staff member or DataSquad student and a researcher. Includes scheduled appointments tracked in LibInsight (Calendly-integrated) and walk-in sign-ins at the DataSquad desk. Excludes canceled appointments (status = Canceled in LibInsight).
Task card A Trello card or GitHub Projects item representing a unit of assigned project work for a DataSquad member. Task cards are not consultations — they represent follow-on or project-based work, often without a direct patron interaction at the time of the task.
Task activity (comment-weighted) A count of comments on task cards, used as a rough workload proxy. This is an activity signal, not equivalent to hours worked, tasks completed, or consultations.
Workshop attendance instance One attendee-event record or one participant-session included in a validated aggregate event count. A person attending three workshops contributes three attendance instances. Aggregate sources without validated affiliation data contribute to overall totals but not UCLA, department, school/division, participant-affiliation, or unique-person metrics.
Organizational parent A broader reporting group assigned only when a record has validated UCLA affiliation and a mapped standardized department. Parents may be a College division, professional school, the Library, UCLA Health, an institute, or an administrative group. Missing and unresolved departments remain unknown.
Dataset (Dataverse) A published data package in UCLA Dataverse — the native Dataverse object that groups related files under a single persistent identifier (DOI).
File (Dataverse) An individual file within a dataset. One dataset may contain one or many files.
Download (Dataverse) A file-level download event recorded by the Dataverse metrics API. Counts include both researcher-initiated and automated/programmatic downloads (e.g., crawlers, API clients) and are not filtered for human-only access.

title: About This Site
text:
Limitations and Caveats

Walk-in undercounting: Walk-in consultations may be undercounted in periods where DataSquad sign-in forms were not consistently used.
Manual log deduplication: Manual LibInsight entries and scheduled exports are deduplicated with a same-provider/same-minute heuristic. A small number of genuine duplicates may remain.
Trello coverage gap: Trello task metrics reflect the period when Trello was the primary DataSquad task system. The transition to GitHub Projects creates a data discontinuity; cross-system comparisons require care.
AWS billing lag: Cost Explorer data for the most recent 1–2 months is an estimate; the relative-share figures may shift after the billing period closes.
Dataverse bot downloads: Download counts are not filtered for automated access. Cumulative totals likely include a fraction of non-human downloads.
Instruction completeness: Workshop attendance completeness depends on consistent LibInsight data entry. Some events may be missing from exports.

UCLA Library Data Science Center. (Year). Research Enabled by DSC. UCLA Library. Retrieved [date] from [site URL].

Named sources for general DSC workshops in 2017-2019 are incomplete, so those years use the published aggregate where it is larger
Aggregates only: row-level registration and attendance data stay outside this repository

title: Metrics Governance (DSC Stats)
text:
Define consistent, reproducible metrics for UCLA Data Science Center reporting across direct consultations, DataSquad task work, and service desk/ticket systems.



Do not mix different units of work into a single metric without explicit labeling.
Examples: - A consultation appointment is not the same as a Trello/GitHub/Jira task. - A task is not the same as a comment/update on a task. - A ticket is not the same as a completed resolution.





These represent direct interactions with patrons/researchers.
Examples: - dsc_consultations_scheduled_count - datasquad_consultations_direct_count - consultations_total_direct_count
Primary sources: - LibInsights / Calendly exports - DataSquad sign-in forms (walk-ins)
Unit: - One consultation record / event row (unless a different rule is explicitly documented)



These represent internal/assigned work performed by DSC/DataSquad, not direct consultations.
Examples: - datasquad_tasks_created_count - datasquad_tasks_completed_count - datasquad_task_activity_comment_count - datasquad_task_activity_comment_weighted_count
Primary sources: - Trello (historical) - GitHub Projects (current/future) - Jira Service Desk / JSM (if used for service requests)
Unit: - Task/card/issue (task_count_*) OR activity on a task (comment_count, update_count)



These represent service requests submitted and tracked in a ticketing system.
Examples: - jsm_tickets_created_count - jsm_tickets_resolved_count - jsm_tickets_open_backlog_count - jsm_ticket_comment_count
Unit: - Ticket/issue or ticket activity



These represent attendance instances at DSC-supported workshops and instructional events.
Primary sources: - Consolidated attendee-level workshop data, including LibInsight and UC-wide event sources - Validated aggregate event summaries when row-level participant data cannot be published
Unit: - One attendee-event row, or one participant-session included in a documented aggregate attendance count
Aggregate event summaries may contribute to overall, year, event, and compatible topic totals. They must not contribute to UCLA affiliation, department, school/division, participant affiliation, or unique-person metrics unless those dimensions are directly supported by validated source data. Missing institution is unknown, not non-UCLA.
Department-level UCLA records may be grouped by organizational_parent using the versioned instruction crosswalk. This broader field includes College divisions, professional schools, the Library, UCLA Health, institutes, external organizations, and administrative groups. Reports must retain parent_type and must not relabel every parent as a school. Missing or unresolved departments remain unknown.




Use names that encode: - who/what (DSC, DataSquad, JSM) - domain (consultations, tasks, tickets) - behavior (created, completed, resolved, direct, activity) - unit (count, comment_count, days)
Examples: - Good: datasquad_trello_task_activity_comment_weighted_count - Good: consultations_direct_count - Bad: total_work (ambiguous)



Every published metric should document: - Source system(s) - Grain/unit (row, card, issue, comment) - Date field used (start_date_time, last_activity_date, created_at, etc.) - Inclusion filters (archived cards, list/status filters, canceled appointments) - Deduplication logic (e.g., Event UUID for LibInsights backfills)
If a rule changes, version it or note the effective date.



Valid: - Direct consultations by year - Task workload by year - Ticket volume by month - Direct consultations vs task workload (side-by-side, separate metrics)
Use caution: - Comparing task activity counts to consultation counts as if they are equivalent output
Not valid (without explicit methodology): - Summing consultations + tasks + comments into one unlabeled “total work” metric



For each period (month/quarter/year), report at least:



DSC direct consultations
DataSquad direct consultations
Total direct consultations





Task count (created/completed)
Task activity (comment/update count or weighted count)
Backlog snapshot (open tasks)





Tickets created
Tickets resolved
Open backlog
Median/average time to resolution (later phase)





When changing systems: - Preserve historical source metrics as-is (Trello) - Add new source metrics (GitHub Projects) - Create a normalized cross-source task metric only after mapping fields and rules - Clearly mark transition dates in dashboards/reports
Do not silently splice two systems together without documentation.




Raw exports are immutable and stored with date-stamped filenames.
Processed datasets are reproducible from scripts.
Reference mappings (staff roster, department map, task filters) live in data/reference/.
Dashboard/report numbers must be traceable to a script and a processed output file.
Restricted participant identifiers must not be copied into public aggregate instruction sources.





Trello “comment-weighted” metrics measure task activity, not direct consultations.
DataSquad sign-in and task sources may have coverage gaps depending on available exports.
Manual consultation logs from Google Drive may overlap with LibInsights and should be used for reconciliation unless dedup rules are implemented.
